claims.claim: **Shame makes OCD hard to disclose.** Explain that the symptoms are involuntary, and tell people troubled by obsessional thoughts that nearly everyone has such thoughts now and then; it is their frequency and distress that mark OCD.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder: treatment (CG31)', published 29 November 2005, last reviewed 11 July 2024 (update in progress), https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg31/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Ask directly in higher-risk groups** (depression, anxiety, alcohol or drug misuse, BDD, eating disorders, dermatology patients): about excessive washing or checking, unwanted thoughts that will not go, daily tasks that take too long, a need for order or distress at mess, and whether these cause trouble.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder: treatment (CG31)', published 29 November 2005, last reviewed 11 July 2024 (update in progress), https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg31/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Assess self-harm and suicide risk, particularly with comorbid depression.** Intrusive sexual, aggressive or death-related thoughts are common in OCD and often wrongly read as dangerous; seek OCD expertise if unsure.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder: treatment (CG31)', published 29 November 2005, last reviewed 11 July 2024 (update in progress), https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg31/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Where family or carers have been drawn into compulsions, avoidance or reassurance-giving,** the plan should help them step back, gently and supportively.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder: treatment (CG31)', published 29 November 2005, last reviewed 11 July 2024 (update in progress), https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg31/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Mild impairment, or a preference for it: low-intensity CBT with ERP** (up to 10 therapist hours), by structured self-help materials, by telephone, or in a group.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder: treatment (CG31)', published 29 November 2005, last reviewed 11 July 2024 (update in progress), https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg31/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Moderate impairment, or mild impairment where low-intensity work failed or was not possible:** let the person choose between an SSRI and more intensive CBT with ERP (over 10 therapist hours); the two work about equally well.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder: treatment (CG31)', published 29 November 2005, last reviewed 11 July 2024 (update in progress), https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg31/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Severe impairment: combine an SSRI with CBT including ERP.**
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder: treatment (CG31)', published 29 November 2005, last reviewed 11 July 2024 (update in progress), https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg31/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **First drug: an SSRI,** namely fluoxetine, fluvoxamine, paroxetine, sertraline or citalopram.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder: treatment (CG31)', published 29 November 2005, last reviewed 11 July 2024 (update in progress), https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg31/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Counsel before starting:** no craving or tolerance; withdrawal symptoms with missed, reduced or stopped doses; side effects that can include more anxiety, suicidal thoughts and self-harm, especially early; a lag of up to 12 weeks before benefit; and medication is not a weakness.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder: treatment (CG31)', published 29 November 2005, last reviewed 11 July 2024 (update in progress), https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg31/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Watch younger adults closely.** Anyone under 30, with comorbid depression or at raised suicide risk needs frequent early monitoring; prescribe small quantities where suicide risk is high, and look actively for akathisia, agitation and new suicidal thinking.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder: treatment (CG31)', published 29 November 2005, last reviewed 11 July 2024 (update in progress), https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg31/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **If a standard dose is not working after 4 to 6 weeks and side effects allow, raise the dose gradually** per the product information, after first checking adherence and alcohol or drug use.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder: treatment (CG31)', published 29 November 2005, last reviewed 11 July 2024 (update in progress), https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg31/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **If the SSRI works, keep it going for 12 months or longer** to prevent relapse, then review; when stopping, taper over several weeks.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder: treatment (CG31)', published 29 November 2005, last reviewed 11 July 2024 (update in progress), https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg31/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Avoid in OCD without comorbidity:** tricyclics other than clomipramine, tricyclic-related drugs, SNRIs (including venlafaxine), MAOIs, and anxiolytics except briefly to cover early SSRI activation. Do not use an antipsychotic on its own.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder: treatment (CG31)', published 29 November 2005, last reviewed 11 July 2024 (update in progress), https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg31/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Not enough benefit from 12 weeks of an SSRI on its own, or from CBT on its own (over 10 therapist hours):** hold a multidisciplinary review, then offer the two combined.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder: treatment (CG31)', published 29 November 2005, last reviewed 11 July 2024 (update in progress), https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg31/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Still not responding after 12 weeks of combined treatment:** offer a different SSRI or clomipramine. Clomipramine is for after at least 1 SSRI has failed or not been tolerated, or when the person prefers it or did well on it before.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder: treatment (CG31)', published 29 November 2005, last reviewed 11 July 2024 (update in progress), https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg31/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Clomipramine safety:** it is toxic in overdose, so supply small amounts when suicide risk is significant; check an ECG and blood pressure first if cardiovascular risk is significant.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder: treatment (CG31)', published 29 November 2005, last reviewed 11 July 2024 (update in progress), https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg31/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Refractory OCD** (an SSRI, combined treatment and clomipramine have all failed): refer to a specialist OCD team. Options, in no proven order, are further CBT or cognitive therapy, antipsychotic augmentation of an SSRI or clomipramine, or clomipramine with citalopram. Primary care should not routinely start combinations or augmentation.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder: treatment (CG31)', published 29 November 2005, last reviewed 11 July 2024 (update in progress), https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg31/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Neurosurgery is not recommended for OCD.**
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder: treatment (CG31)', published 29 November 2005, last reviewed 11 July 2024 (update in progress), https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg31/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Psychological treatment first.** Mild impairment: guided self-help with family support may be tried. Moderate to severe impairment, or when self-help has failed: CBT with ERP, involving the family and adapted to the child's developmental age.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder: treatment (CG31)', published 29 November 2005, last reviewed 11 July 2024 (update in progress), https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg31/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Adding an SSRI to CBT after multidisciplinary review** (moderate to severe impairment, inadequate CBT response): consider it at ages 8 to 11, offer it at 12 to 18. A child and adolescent psychiatrist should assess first. Use sertraline or fluvoxamine, or fluoxetine if there is significant comorbid depression.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder: treatment (CG31)', published 29 November 2005, last reviewed 11 July 2024 (update in progress), https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg31/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Prescribing for children:** start low (a half or quarter of the usual starting dose may be used for the first week); warn families about suicidal behaviour, self-harm or hostility; continue a successful SSRI for 6 months or more after remission; and do an ECG before clomipramine.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder: treatment (CG31)', published 29 November 2005, last reviewed 11 July 2024 (update in progress), https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg31/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Follow up for a year after remission**, then discharge to primary care if recovery holds. Relapse is common, so see re-referred people promptly rather than putting them on a routine waiting list.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder: treatment (CG31)', published 29 November 2005, last reviewed 11 July 2024 (update in progress), https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg31/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23
